Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): This is an appeal of a December 9, 2019 decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (Board) denying the Appellant's claim for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c. 27 (IRPA).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: This is an appeal of a December 9, 2019 decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (Board) denying the Appellant's claim for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c. 27 (IRPA).

The Appellant, a Ukrainian national, claims that, in 2002, he joined the Party of Regions and became the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in the village of XXXX. After president Victor Yanukovych-the Party's candidate who had been elected president in 2010 -was ousted in the February 2014 revolution, members of the Party were persecuted and, on XXXX XXXX, 2014, the Appellant was beaten by two masked men, leading to his hospitalization for six days.

On XXXX XXXX, 2015, after meeting about the possible participation of the Party in the 2015 municipal election, the Appellant claims he was beaten by unknown assailants, leading to his hospitalization for 14 days. Finally, on XXXX XXXX, 2017 (either in the afternoon or late at night1), the Appellant was beaten by unknown assailants and hospitalized for 16 days, after preparing the registration documents for a candidate from the Party. After each attack, he contacted the police, but they were unable to assist.

As a result of the XXXX 2017 attack, he applied for a Canadian visitor visa, which was issued on XXXX XXXX, 2017. On XXXX XXXX, 2017 he flew from Ukraine to Toronto, leaving behind his wife and two children. He claims that if he returns to Ukraine, he will face persecution from the "political bloc of Petr Poroshenko," president of Ukraine from June 2014 until April 2019.
For the reasons that follow, I deny this appeal.

The Appellant has included in his appeal record the several news article (or excepts therefrom), one of which is dated September 30, 2019; one of which is dated June 21, 2019; and the balance of which are undated.2
paragraphs.heading_before: REQUEST FOR THE ADMISSION OF NEW EVIDENCE

paragraphs.text: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA limits the admission of evidence in an appeal before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to evidence that: 1) arose after the RPD's rejection of the claim; 2) was not reasonably available at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim; or 3) an appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the RPD's rejection of the claim. The evidence must also meet the factors elaborated by the Federal Court of Appeal in the Singh case3 (where the Court relied on its earlier finding in the Raza case4), i.e. newness, credibility, relevance, and a modified version of materiality.5

RAD Rule 3(3)(g)(iii)6 provides that an appellant seeking the admission of new evidence must provide full and detailed submissions regarding how the evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the appellant.

The full and detailed submissions required by RAD Rule 3(3)(g)(iii) have not been provided.7 The Appellant's only reference to the documents pertains to their relevance: "We provided the Penal [sic] with the current violent country conditions in Ukraine confirming the ongoing persecution and threats to the followers of the Party of Region in the county. The new relevant proofs are enclosed to this Appeal."8
Because the Appellant has not made submissions as to how the documents comply with subsection 110(4), I find that they are inadmissible.9

In the alternative, in case my call for adherence to the rules is viewed as overly exigent, I will consider the evidence with a view to determining if its content self-evidently meets the requirements of subsection 110(4). I note that all of the articles are dated before the rejection of the claim by the RPD or are undated; as such they may not be said to have arisen after the rejection of the claim. Nor is there any indication that they were not reasonably available as of that date. I find that they do not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) and, as such, are inadmissible.
The Appellant has requested a hearing in relation to the new evidence. Because no new evidence has been admitted, the request for a hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA must be denied.
In my review of the RPD's decision, I will apply a standard of correctness.10 This is not a case where the RPD enjoyed a meaningful advantage in making its findings.11 ANALYSIS

The RPD held as follows: 1) The Appellant's evidence that he had been persecuted in the past due to his political activities was speculative. When asked if the attacks were political, he testified that he overheard one of his attackers saying: "Please do not stick your nose in things that you shouldn't stick his nose into."12 When asked by the RPD member if there was anything else about the assaults that caused him to think that they were related to his politics, he testified: "Yes, this was related to my membership in the party."13 2) The Appellant had the following credibility problems: a) his answers were, at times, non-responsive; b) he was vague and evasive in his testimony, in particular in his attempt to explain that he had to hire someone to arrange for a visa for him (based on false information) because the Ukrainian government was preventing the Canadian government from issuing visas to Party of Regions supporters; c) his claimed employment history was contradictory (in his port of entry notes he said he worked for the XXXX of former president Yanukovych, in his testimony he said that before coming to Canada he worked in XXXX with his son and for XXXX, and in his Schedule A form he said that he held a XXXX position working as a "XXXX XXXX" for former president Yanukovych from XXXX 2013 to XXXX 2014); and d) he lacked evidence from Party officials showing he was a member and that he had been attacked, which should have been reasonably available. 3) His supporting evidence was deficient: a) his claim that his wife's health problems were linked to his treatment in Ukraine was not supported by the medical reports or by common sense (rheumatoid arthritis is not caused by being married to someone who has been persecuted); b) a doctor's note stating that he has experienced depression and anxiety warranted no weight because it does not support his claim about what happened in Ukraine and it is not clear what it is based on; and c) two handwritten letters from people who allege that they are friends of his and Party members deserve no weight because there were no identity documents accompanying them and the RPD had no independent verification of the authors' identity. 4) As to a general profile, while there is country condition evidence that there was violence among Party supporters in connection with the popular uprising in 2014, there was no evidence to support his claim that ordinary Party members continue to be individually targeted years afterwards.

The Appellant makes the following arguments in reply to the RPD's findings.14 1) In reply to the RPD's finding at 2(d), he argues that he could not get supporting evidence from the Party because after the 2014 overthrow, the Party was dispersed and the documentation was destroyed: "political and information censorship swept over Ukraine and there are no possibilities to obtain the updated documents."15 2) In reply to the RPD's finding 4, he argues that it erred in stating that the Appellant had not established he was persecuted in the past or has a political profile that would support his allegation that he would be targeted in the future based upon his past. The Appellant argues that since the 2014 overthrow, civil resistance and disobedience in Ukraine has grown, resulting in new street fights and persecution of Party members. He states that this is shown by the country condition evidence provided to the RPD and the new evidence submitted with this appeal. 3) In response to the RPD's findings at 2(a) and (b), he argues that he was not unresponsive, vague, or evasive. Rather, he had psychological conditions and took medications that caused difficulties in his communication skills-as shown by a certificate from his family doctor. 4) In response to the RPD's finding at 2(c), he argues that the RPD erred in finding inconsistencies about where he worked. There was an interpretation error because "work" in the Ukrainian language means only "permanent employment, making money."16 His political activity as a member of the Party was on a voluntary basis. 5) In response to the RPD's finding at 3(a) and (b), he argues that the medical certificates he provided to the RPD "confirm [that] the medical conditions of his wife and himself have started after the threats and persecutions of 2014-2016 and the diagnosis of hypertension, depression, and anxiety are directly related to the serious concerns of the life and health of the claimants and his family members."17

I find as follows: 1) While it is clear from the evidence that the Party of Regions suffered serious losses in 2014, there is no evidence that it ceased to exist at that time. Indeed, according to the Appellant's own evidence, the attacks against him in 2015 and 2017 were both related to his efforts in support of Party candidates. Nor is there any evidence regarding the destruction of Party documents or the lack of archives. (Clearly the memorandum is not a means by which the Appellant's counsel may introduce evidence of her view of the state of affairs in Ukraine.) I note further that the evidence does not show that the Appellant made any attempt to obtain evidence from former Party officials-something he did do with former Party members.18 2) As noted above, the new evidence which the Appellant requested the admission of has been found inadmissible. Based on my review of the country condition evidence as contained in the National Documentation Package (NDP), as well as the extracts of news articles provided by the Appellant to the RPD,19 I agree with the RPD that the objective evidence does not support his claim that a party member at his level would be targeted into the future. 3) A XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019 letter from a walk-in clinic in XXXX, Ontario states that the Appellant "complains about anxiety and depression with migraine headache and panic attack [sic]" and notes that he has been prescribed anti-depressants.20 In addition, the doctor states "I advised him of not returning [sic] to Ukraine as that will endanger his life." First, I note that no link between the Appellant's conditions and his ability to testify coherently and directly is made in the letter. Moreover, I note that the doctor's statement about the risk to the Appellant in Ukraine-a statement made without any supporting reasoning and outside his area of expertise-undermines the overall value of the letter. It shows that the letter's author, instead of providing evidence as a neutral expert, has become an advocate of the Appellant, or at the very least shown a willingness to provide non-medical opinions in a medical letter. Without evidence that the Appellant had a medical condition that would result in testimony that was unresponsive, vague, or evasive, I am unable to find that his mental health provides a justification for the nature of his testimony. Aside from statements by his counsel at the hearing about the nature of his personality and her comments in the memorandum, there is no indication that he has any such condition. Again, it is not appropriate for the Appellant's counsel to offer evidence. I agree with the RPD's assessment of the quality of his testimony. 4) Once again, the Appellant's counsel appears to believe that a legal memorandum represents an opportunity for her to provide evidence-this time about the proper translation of certain words from Ukrainian into English. I am unable to accept arguments about the quality of the translation in the absence of evidence that it was faulty. Moreover, even accepting that the Appellant worked as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in his village on a full-time basis or non-remunerative basis (and that "XXXX XXXX of Vasyl Ivanochko in XXXX";21 "XXXX XXXX" for Yanukovych;22 and "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX"23 are all the same job), his testimony about when he undertook the work is inconsistent. According to his testimony, he worked for the XXXX organization, which was "part of the XXXX XXXX,"24 from 2010 to 2014 "and after [2014] I did not work anymore....I was doing XXXX with my son."25 He also submitted a letter from a friend (and member of the Party) stating that he had ceased working as a XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2014.26 However, this contradicts another supporting letter he provided, which certifies that he had been employed in the position of XXXX XXXX for the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX from XXXX XXXX, 2010 to XXXX XXXX, 2015.27 I agree with the RPD that the unexplained lack of consistency by the Appellant regarding his employment history undermines his credibility and find that he did not, in fact, work as a XXXX of former president Yanukovych or the XXXX in his village. 5) As regards the medical records of the Appellant's wife, these do not provide any link whatsoever between her various illnesses (XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) and the Appellant's alleged attacks. The fact that they pertain to time periods that overlap with the Appellant's alleged abuse, does not link her conditions to that alleged abuse. The reports relating to the Appellant's health do provide support for his claim to have been attacked and hospitalized: * a 2014 report28 indicates a period of hospitalization, corresponding with the date he gave for the 2014 attack, notes a severe head injury and states the patient "claims he was attacked by unknown individuals wearing masks...;" * a 2015 report29 indicates a period of hospitalization corresponding with the date he gave for the 2015 attack and notes a severe injury; and, * a 2017 report30 notes a severe head injury, indicates a period of hospitalization corresponding with the date he gave for the 2017 attack, and notes that the patient "complained about being attacked by strangers on XXXX XXXX XXXX.2017." I will have regard to these reports in my overall assessment of the claim. I note, however, that even if the attacks did occur, there is nothing in this supporting evidence or (as per the RPD's uncontested finding 1) above) in the Appellant's own evidence, that provides a clear link between his alleged activities on behalf of the Party and the attacks.

I have considered the Appellant's credibility problems-including the lack of reasonably available documentation without reasonable explanation; the evasive and non-responsive nature of his testimony, in particular about the interference of the Ukrainian state with the ability of members of the Party to obtain Canadian visas;31 and the inconsistency in the Appellant's evidence about when he worked as an XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX-and the dearth of evidence showing that he had been subjected to persecution based on his political views or that he was likely to be persecuted in the future. When I weigh this against the supporting evidence that does exist, I find that there is not a serious possibility that he will face persecution or a likelihood of other harm upon his return to Ukraine.

The Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a protected person. The appeal is dismissed.
